en.content: The reaction A(g) + 2B(g) → C(g) is an elementary reaction. In an experiment involving this reaction, the initial partial pressures of A and B are $P_A = 0.40$ atm and $P_B = 1.0$ atm respectively. When pressure of C becomes $0.3$ atm in the reaction the rate of the reaction relative to the initial rate is:
en.explanation:
For an elementary reaction,

$$ A(g)+2B(g)\rightarrow C(g) $$

the rate law is written directly from the molecularity:

$$ r=kP_A(P_B)^2 $$

Initial rate:

$$ r_0=k(0.40)(1.0)^2 $$

$$ r_0=0.40k $$

Now, when the partial pressure of $C$ becomes $0.3$ atm, it means $0.3$ atm of $C$ has formed.

From the reaction,

$$ A+2B\rightarrow C $$

For every $1$ atm of $C$ formed:

  • $1$ atm of $A$ is used

  • $2$ atm of $B$ are used

So for $0.3$ atm of $C$ formed:

$$ P_A \text{ used}=0.3 \text{ atm} $$

$$ P_B \text{ used}=2(0.3)=0.6 \text{ atm} $$

New partial pressures:

$$ P_A=0.40-0.30=0.10 \text{ atm} $$

$$ P_B=1.0-0.60=0.40 \text{ atm} $$

Rate at this stage:

$$ r=k(0.10)(0.40)^2 $$

$$ r=k(0.10)(0.16)=0.016k $$

So the rate relative to the initial rate is

$$ \frac{r}{r_0}=\frac{0.016k}{0.40k} $$

$$ \frac{r}{r_0}=0.04=\frac{1}{25} $$

So the correct option is

$$ \boxed{\frac{1}{25}} $$

Option C.

en.content:
The rate law for the dimerisation of NO2 is

$$-\frac{d[NO_2]}{dt} = k [NO_2]^2$$

Which of the following changes will change the value of the specific rate constant, $k$:

options.content: Doubling the total pressure on the system

en.explanation:
The correct option is Option B: Doubling the temperature.

For the dimerisation of $NO_2$, the rate law is

$$ -\frac{d[NO_2]}{dt}=k[NO_2]^2 $$

Here, $k$ is the specific rate constant.

For a given reaction, the value of $k$ does not depend on the concentration or pressure of reactants. It depends mainly on:

  • temperature

  • nature of reactants

  • catalyst, if present

If we double the total pressure of the system, the concentration of $NO_2$ may change, so the rate of reaction may change. But the value of $k$ remains the same, provided temperature is constant.

On the other hand, if we double the temperature, the value of $k$ changes. According to the Arrhenius equation,

$$ k=Ae^{-E_a/RT} $$

So $k$ depends on temperature.

Hence, the change that will change the value of the specific rate constant is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option B: Doubling the temperature}} $$

en.content: A graph plotted between $\log \mathrm{t}_{50 \%}$ vs. log concentration is a straight line. What conclusion can you draw from this graph.
en.explanation:
For an $n^{\text{th}}$ order reaction, the relationship between the half-life ($t_{1/2}$ or $t_{50\%}$) and the initial concentration ($a$) is given by:

$$t_{1/2} \propto \frac{1}{a^{n-1}}$$

$$t_{1/2} = \text{constant} \times a^{1-n}$$

$$\log t_{50\%} = \log(\text{constant}) + (1 - n)\log a$$

This acts as the equation of a straight line, $y = mx + c$, where:

$y = \log t_{50\%}$

$x = \log a$ (log concentration)

Slope ($m$) = $1 - n$

In standard chemical kinetic graphs plotted this way, the straight line is parallel to the horizontal axis (the log concentration axis), which implies that the slope of the line is zero.

By equating the slope to zero, we get:

$$1 - n = 0$$

$$n = 1$$

This tells us that it is a first-order reaction. A key characteristic of a first-order reaction is that its half-life remains constant and is entirely independent of the initial concentration. The formula for the half-life of a first-order reaction is given by:

$$t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}$$

Now we can evaluate the given choices based on our findings:

  • Option C gives $n = 1$ and $t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}$. This accurately matches our derivation for a first-order reaction shown by a horizontal line.

Option C is the correct conclusion.

en.content:
The forward rate constant for the elementary reversible gaseous reaction

C2H6 → 2CH3 is $1.57 \times 10^{-3}$ s−1 at 100 K

What is the rate constant for the backward reaction at this temperature if $10^{-4}$ mole of CH3 and 10 moles of C2H6 are present in a 10 litre vessel at equilibrium?
en.explanation:
For the reversible elementary reaction,

$$ \mathrm{C_2H_6 \rightleftharpoons 2CH_3} $$

Forward reaction:

$$ \mathrm{C_2H_6 \rightarrow 2CH_3} $$

Since it is elementary, the rate of forward reaction is

$$ r_f = k_f[\mathrm{C_2H_6}] $$

Backward reaction:

$$ \mathrm{2CH_3 \rightarrow C_2H_6} $$

So the rate of backward reaction is

$$ r_b = k_b[\mathrm{CH_3}]^2 $$

At equilibrium, forward rate = backward rate.

$$ k_f[\mathrm{C_2H_6}] = k_b[\mathrm{CH_3}]^2 $$

Given:

$$ k_f = 1.57 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

Volume of vessel $= 10\ \mathrm{L}$

Concentration of $\mathrm{C_2H_6}$:

$$ [\mathrm{C_2H_6}] = \frac{10}{10} = 1\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}} $$

Concentration of $\mathrm{CH_3}$:

$$ [\mathrm{CH_3}] = \frac{10^{-4}}{10} = 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}} $$

Now substitute in the equilibrium rate relation:

$$ 1.57 \times 10^{-3} \times 1 = k_b(10^{-5})^2 $$

$$ 1.57 \times 10^{-3} = k_b \times 10^{-10} $$

$$ k_b = \frac{1.57 \times 10^{-3}}{10^{-10}} $$

$$ k_b = 1.57 \times 10^7\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}\ s^{-1}} $$

So the correct option is:

$$ \boxed{1.57 \times 10^7\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}\ s^{-1}}} $$

Option D.

en.content: Rate constant $k$ is $2.303$ min$^{-1}$ for a particular reaction. The initial concentration of the reaction is $1$ mole/litre. Then rate of reaction after 1 minute is:
en.explanation:
Since the unit of rate constant is $\text{min}^{-1}$, the reaction is a first order reaction.

For a first order reaction,

$$ [A] = [A]_0 e^{-kt} $$

Given,

$$ [A]_0 = 1 \text{ mol L}^{-1} $$

$$ k = 2.303 \text{ min}^{-1} $$

$$ t = 1 \text{ min} $$

So,

$$ [A] = 1 \times e^{-2.303 \times 1} $$

Since $2.303 = \ln 10$,

$$ e^{-2.303} = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1 $$

So after $1$ minute,

$$ [A] = 0.1 \text{ M} $$

For a first order reaction, rate is

$$ \text{Rate} = k[A] $$

$$ \text{Rate} = 2.303 \times 0.1 $$

$$ \text{Rate} = 0.2303 \text{ M min}^{-1} $$

So the correct option is:

$$ \boxed{0.2303 \text{ M min}^{-1}} $$

Option B.

en.content: For an elementary reaction $2A + B \rightarrow A_2B$, if the volume of vessel is quickly reduced to half of its original volume, then rate of reaction will -
en.explanation:
For an elementary reaction,

$$ 2A + B \rightarrow A_2B $$

the rate law is written directly from the stoichiometric coefficients:

$$ \text{Rate} = k[A]^2[B] $$

Now, the volume of the vessel is quickly reduced to half.

Since concentration is

$$ \text{Concentration} = \frac{\text{moles}}{\text{volume}} $$

when volume becomes half, the concentration of each reactant becomes double.

So,

$$ [A]' = 2[A] $$

and

$$ [B]' = 2[B] $$

New rate:

$$ \text{Rate}' = k(2[A])^2(2[B]) $$

$$ \text{Rate}' = k \cdot 4[A]^2 \cdot 2[B] $$

$$ \text{Rate}' = 8k[A]^2[B] $$

So the rate becomes $8$ times the original rate.

The correct option is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option C: increase eight times}} $$

en.content: For a first order reaction A → B + 2C + 3D (A is optically inactive and B, C and D are dextrorotary), the optical rotation at time t and ∞ are $r_t$ and $r_{\infty}$ respectively, the expression for rate constant is
en.explanation:
For a first order reaction,

$$ A \rightarrow B + 2C + 3D $$

$A$ is optically inactive, so it does not contribute to optical rotation.

The products $B, C$ and $D$ are dextrorotary, so as the reaction proceeds, optical rotation increases due to formation of products.

For a first order reaction, if initial concentration of $A$ is $a$ and amount reacted at time $t$ is $x$, then

$$ k = \frac{1}{t}\ln \frac{a}{a-x} $$

Now, optical rotation is proportional to the amount of products formed.

At time $t$:

$$ r_t \propto x $$

At infinite time, the reaction is complete:

$$ r_{\infty} \propto a $$

So,

$$ r_{\infty} - r_t \propto a-x $$

Substituting these in the first order rate expression:

$$ k = \frac{1}{t}\ln \frac{r_{\infty}}{r_{\infty}-r_t} $$

So the correct expression is

$$ \boxed{k = \frac{1}{t}\ln \frac{r_{\infty}}{r_{\infty}-r_t}} $$

Correct option: B

en.content: The reaction A(g) + 2B(g) → C(g) + D(g) is an elementary process. In an experiment, the initial partial pressure of A and B are $P_A = 0.60$ and $P_B = 0.80$ atm. When $P_C = 0.2$ atm, the rate of reaction relative to the initial rate is :
en.explanation:
For an elementary reaction,

$$ A(g)+2B(g)\rightarrow C(g)+D(g) $$

the rate law is written directly from the stoichiometric coefficients:

$$ r=kP_A(P_B)^2 $$

Initially,

$$ P_A=0.60\ \text{atm},\qquad P_B=0.80\ \text{atm} $$

So the initial rate is

$$ r_0=k(0.60)(0.80)^2 $$

Now, when

$$ P_C=0.20\ \text{atm} $$

it means $0.20$ atm of $C$ has been formed.

From the reaction,

$$ A+2B\rightarrow C+D $$

For every $1$ part of $C$ formed, $1$ part of $A$ is used and $2$ parts of $B$ are used.

So,

$$ P_A=0.60-0.20=0.40\ \text{atm} $$

and

$$ P_B=0.80-2(0.20)=0.40\ \text{atm} $$

Rate at this moment:

$$ r=k(0.40)(0.40)^2 $$

Now compare with the initial rate:

$$ \frac{r}{r_0} = \frac{k(0.40)(0.40)^2}{k(0.60)(0.80)^2} $$

$$ \frac{r}{r_0} = \frac{0.40\times 0.16}{0.60\times 0.64} $$

$$ \frac{r}{r_0} = \frac{0.064}{0.384} = \frac{1}{6} $$

So the rate of reaction relative to the initial rate is

$$ \boxed{\frac{1}{6}} $$

Correct option: D.

en.content:
In the following reaction, how is the rate of appearance of the underlined product related to rate of disappearance of the underlined reactant:

BrO3-(aq) + 5 Br-(aq) + 6H+(aq) → 3 Br2(l) + 3H2O(l)
en.explanation:
For the reaction,

$$ BrO_3^-(aq) + 5Br^-(aq) + 6H^+(aq) \rightarrow 3Br_2(l) + 3H_2O(l) $$

The stoichiometric coefficients tell us how fast substances are consumed or formed.

Here, $5$ moles of $Br^-$ disappear to form $3$ moles of $Br_2$.

So the rate relation is:

$$ -\frac{1}{5}\frac{d[Br^-]}{dt}=\frac{1}{3}\frac{d[Br_2]}{dt} $$

Now rearrange:

$$ \frac{d[Br_2]}{dt}=-\frac{3}{5}\frac{d[Br^-]}{dt} $$

The negative sign is because $Br^-$ is a reactant, so its concentration decreases with time.

So the correct option is:

$$ \boxed{\frac{d[Br_2]}{dt}=-\frac{3}{5}\frac{d[Br^-]}{dt}} $$

Option D.

en.content: Which of the following is not a instantaneous reaction?

options.content: Precipitation of BaSO4 when solution of BaCl2 and H2SO4 are mixed.
Precipitation of AgCl when solutions of silver nitrate and NaCl are mixed.

en.explanation:
The reaction which is not instantaneous is:

Option D: Rusting of iron

Neutralisation of an acid with a base is very fast. For example,

$$ \text{HCl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} $$

Precipitation reactions like formation of $\text{BaSO}_4$ and $\text{AgCl}$ also occur immediately when the two solutions are mixed.

$$ \text{BaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4 \downarrow + 2\text{HCl} $$

$$ \text{AgNO}_3 + \text{NaCl} \rightarrow \text{AgCl} \downarrow + \text{NaNO}_3 $$

But rusting of iron is a slow process. It takes a long time because iron reacts slowly with oxygen and moisture present in air.

So, the correct answer is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option D: Rusting of iron}} $$

en.content: For the zero order reaction $A \rightarrow B + C$; initial concentration of A is 0.1 M. If $[A] = 0.08$ M after 10 min, then its half-life and completion time are respectively.
en.explanation:
For a zero order reaction, the integrated rate equation is

$$ [A] = [A]_0 - kt $$

Given,

$$ [A]_0 = 0.1\,M $$

and after $10$ min,

$$ [A] = 0.08\,M $$

So,

$$ 0.08 = 0.1 - k(10) $$

$$ 10k = 0.1 - 0.08 = 0.02 $$

$$ k = \frac{0.02}{10} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\,M\,min^{-1} $$

For a zero order reaction, half-life is

$$ t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k} $$

$$ t_{1/2} = \frac{0.1}{2 \times 2 \times 10^{-3}} $$

$$ t_{1/2} = \frac{0.1}{4 \times 10^{-3}} = 25\,min $$

Completion time means the time when $[A] = 0$.

Using

$$ [A] = [A]_0 - kt $$

$$ 0 = 0.1 - (2 \times 10^{-3})t $$

$$ t = \frac{0.1}{2 \times 10^{-3}} = 50\,min $$

So, the half-life and completion time are respectively

$$ 25\,min \text{ and } 50\,min $$

Correct option: C.

en.content: At room temperature, the reaction between NO and O2 to give NO2 is fast, while that between CO and O2 is slow. It is due to :

options.content: CO is smaller in size than that of NO
The activation energy for the reaction, $2NO + O_2 \rightarrow 2NO_2$ is less than $2CO + O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2$.

en.explanation:
Correct option: C

The reaction

$$ 2NO + O_2 \rightarrow 2NO_2 $$

is fast at room temperature because it has a lower activation energy.

Activation energy is the minimum energy required for reacting molecules to form products. If activation energy is low, a larger number of molecules can cross the energy barrier even at room temperature, so the reaction is fast.

For carbon monoxide,

$$ 2CO + O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2 $$

the activation energy is higher. So, at room temperature, only a small number of molecules have enough energy to react. That is why this reaction is slow, even though it is thermodynamically favourable.

Option A is not correct because the size of CO and NO is not the main reason for the difference in reaction rate.

Option B is also not correct because the poisonous nature of CO does not decide how fast it reacts with oxygen.

So, the correct answer is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option C}} $$

en.content:
The mechanism of the reaction, 2NO + O2 → 2NO2 is

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{NO}+\mathrm{NO} \underset{\mathrm{k}_{-1}}{\stackrel{\mathrm{k}_1}{\rightleftharpoons}} \mathrm{~N}_2 \mathrm{O}_2 \text { (fast) ; } \\ & \mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_2+\mathrm{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\mathrm{k}_2} 2 \mathrm{NO}_2 \text { (slow) ; }\end{aligned}$

The rate constant of the reaction is :
en.explanation:
For the given mechanism,

$$ \mathrm{NO}+\mathrm{NO} \underset{k_{-1}}{\stackrel{k_1}{\rightleftharpoons}} \mathrm{N_2O_2} $$

This first step is fast, so it is treated as an equilibrium step.

For the fast equilibrium,

$$ k_1[\mathrm{NO}]^2 = k_{-1}[\mathrm{N_2O_2}] $$

So,

$$ [\mathrm{N_2O_2}] = \frac{k_1}{k_{-1}}[\mathrm{NO}]^2 $$

The slow step decides the rate of the reaction:

$$ \mathrm{N_2O_2}+\mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow{k_2} 2\mathrm{NO_2} $$

So the rate is

$$ \text{Rate} = k_2[\mathrm{N_2O_2}][\mathrm{O_2}] $$

Substitute the value of $[\mathrm{N_2O_2}]$:

$$ \text{Rate} = k_2 \left(\frac{k_1}{k_{-1}}\right)[\mathrm{NO}]^2[\mathrm{O_2}] $$

So the overall rate constant is

$$ k = k_2\left(\frac{k_1}{k_{-1}}\right) $$

Hence, the correct option is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option D } \; k_2\left(\frac{k_1}{k_{-1}}\right)} $$

en.content: If the initial concentration of reactants in certain reaction is double, the half-life period of the reaction doubles, the order of a reaction is :
en.explanation:
For a zero order reaction, the half-life is given by

$$ t_{1/2}=\frac{[R]_0}{2k} $$

Here, $[R]_0$ is the initial concentration of the reactant.

So, for a zero order reaction,

$$ t_{1/2} \propto [R]_0 $$

This means if the initial concentration is doubled, the half-life also becomes double.

Given in the question:

Initial concentration doubles $\Rightarrow$ half-life doubles.

This matches the zero order reaction.

So, the order of the reaction is

$$ \boxed{\text{Zero}} $$

Correct option: A.

hi.content: यदि किसी निश्चित अभिक्रिया में अभिकारकों की प्रारंभिक सांद्रता दोगुनी कर दी जाती है, तो अभिक्रिया का अर्ध-आयु काल दोगुना हो जाता है, अभिक्रिया की कोटि है :

en.content:
Consider the following statements

I. $[A] = -kt + [A]_0$ is the equation for zero order reaction.

II. In graphical method, data are plotted according to integrated rate equations for different order reactions.

III. In initial rate method, initial rate number is determined either numerically or from the slope of the curve vs time.

IV. Integrated rate method is also known as hit and trial method.

Choose the correct statements and tick the correct option
en.explanation:
Statement I is correct.

For a zero order reaction,

$$ -\frac{d[A]}{dt}=k $$

On integration,

$$ [A]=[A]_0-kt $$

This can also be written as

$$ [A]=-kt+[A]_0 $$

So statement I is true.

Statement II is also correct.

In the graphical method, we plot the experimental data according to the integrated rate equations of different order reactions. The plot which gives a straight line helps us identify the order of reaction.

Statement III is correct.

In the initial rate method, the initial rate of reaction can be found either numerically or from the slope of the concentration vs time curve at the beginning of the reaction.

Statement IV is also correct.

The integrated rate method is also called the hit and trial method because we try different integrated rate equations and check which one fits the data properly.

So all the given statements are correct.

$$ \boxed{\text{Option D: All of these}} $$

en.content: Which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.content: The catalyst does not affect the equilibrium of a reaction.
Reaction with higher activation energy has higher rate constant.
In an exothermic reaction, the activation energy of the reverse reaction is higher than that of the forward reaction.
Half-life period of a first order reaction is independent of initial concentration.

en.explanation:
The incorrect statement is:

Option B: Reaction with higher activation energy has higher rate constant.

According to Arrhenius equation,

$$ k = A e^{-E_a/RT} $$

where $k$ is the rate constant and $E_a$ is the activation energy.

From this relation, if activation energy $E_a$ is higher, the value of $e^{-E_a/RT}$ becomes smaller. So the rate constant $k$ decreases.

This means a reaction with higher activation energy generally has a lower rate constant, not a higher one.

The other statements are correct:

  • A catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant or the position of equilibrium. It only helps the reaction reach equilibrium faster.

  • In an exothermic reaction, the reverse reaction has higher activation energy than the forward reaction.

  • For a first order reaction,

$$ t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k} $$

so the half-life is independent of initial concentration.

So, the incorrect statement is Option B.

en.content: The rate constant ($k'$) of one of the reaction is found to be double that of the rate constant ($k''$) of another reaction. Then, the relationship between the corresponding activation energies of the two reactions ($E_a'$ and $E_a''$) can be represented as
en.explanation:
The correct option is B:

$$E_a' < E_a''$$

According to the Arrhenius equation,

$$k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$$

Here,

  • $k$ is the rate constant,

  • $E_a$ is the activation energy,

  • $R$ is the gas constant,

  • $T$ is the temperature,

  • $A$ is the frequency factor.

For reactions compared at the same temperature, the rate constant depends inversely on activation energy.

A reaction with lower activation energy has more molecules able to cross the energy barrier, so its rate constant is higher.

Given:

$$k' = 2k''$$

So the first reaction has a higher rate constant than the second reaction. Hence, its activation energy must be lower.

$$E_a' < E_a''$$

So, the answer is Option B.

hi.content: एक अभिक्रिया का दर नियतांक ($k'$) किसी अन्य अभिक्रिया के दर नियतांक ($k''$) का दोगुना पाया जाता है। तब, दोनों अभिक्रियाओं की संगत सक्रियण ऊर्जाओं ($E_a'$ और $E_a''$) के बीच के संबंध को इस प्रकार दर्शाया जा सकता है:

en.content:
Statement I : For zero-order reaction (A → B), successive half-life of reaction decreases with the progress of reaction.

Statement II : Rate of zero-order reaction remains unchanged with the progress of reaction.

options.content: If both statements are CORRECT, and Statement  II is the CORRECT explanation of Statement I.
If both statements are CORRECT, and Statement  II is NOT the CORRECT explanation of  Statement I.
If Statement I is CORRECT, but Statement II is  INCORRECT.
If Statement I is INCORRECT, but Statement II  is CORRECT.

en.explanation:
For a zero-order reaction,

$$ A \rightarrow B $$

the rate law is

$$ \text{Rate} = k[A]^0 = k $$

So, the rate of reaction remains constant as the reaction proceeds. It does not depend on the concentration of $A$.

Now, for a zero-order reaction, the integrated rate equation is

$$ [A] = [A]_0 - kt $$

The half-life is

$$ t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k} $$

This shows that half-life depends directly on the concentration of reactant present.

As the reaction progresses, the concentration of $A$ decreases. So the time required to reduce the remaining concentration to half also decreases.

For example, if the concentration changes:

$$ [A]_0 \rightarrow \frac{[A]_0}{2} $$

the first half-life is

$$ \frac{[A]_0}{2k} $$

Next, for

$$ \frac{[A]_0}{2} \rightarrow \frac{[A]_0}{4} $$

the time taken is

$$ \frac{[A]_0}{4k} $$

which is smaller.

So, successive half-lives decrease with the progress of a zero-order reaction.

Statement I is correct.

Statement II is also correct.

Also, Statement II correctly explains Statement I because the constant rate means smaller amounts of reactant are consumed in smaller times.

Hence, the correct option is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option A}} $$

en.content: Decomposition of NH3 over a tungsten surface obeys zero-order kinetics. For an initial pressure of 70 mm of NH3, its half-life is 315 s. What will be the half-life if the initial pressure is 150 mm?
en.explanation:
For a zero-order reaction, the half-life is directly proportional to the initial concentration or initial pressure.

For zero-order kinetics,

$$ t_{1/2}=\frac{[A]_0}{2k} $$

Since pressure is proportional to concentration, we can write:

$$ t_{1/2} \propto P_0 $$

So,

$$ \frac{t_2}{t_1}=\frac{P_2}{P_1} $$

Given:

$$ t_1=315\ \text{s}, \quad P_1=70\ \text{mm} $$

and

$$ P_2=150\ \text{mm} $$

So,

$$ t_2=315 \times \frac{150}{70} $$

$$ t_2=315 \times \frac{15}{7} $$

$$ t_2=45 \times 15=675\ \text{s} $$

So, the half-life would be

$$ \boxed{675\ \text{s}} $$

Correct option: C.

en.content:
How many of the following statements are correct?

(1) unit of rate of disapperarance is $\mathrm{Ms}^{-1}$

(2) Unit of rate of reaction is $\mathrm{Ms}^{-1}$

(3) Unit of rate constant $k$ is depend on order

(4) Unit of k for first order reaction is $\mathrm{Ms}^{-1}$
en.explanation:
The correct statements are (1), (2), and (3).

Rate of disappearance of a reactant means change in concentration of reactant per unit time.

So its unit is:

$$ \frac{\text{mol L}^{-1}}{\text{s}}=\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1} $$

Since $\text{mol L}^{-1}$ is also written as $\mathrm{M}$, the unit becomes:

$$ \mathrm{M s}^{-1} $$

So statement (1) is correct.

Rate of reaction also has the unit of concentration per unit time, so its unit is also:

$$ \mathrm{M s}^{-1} $$

So statement (2) is correct.

The unit of rate constant $k$ depends on the order of reaction.

For a reaction of order $n$:

$$ \text{Rate}=k[A]^n $$

So,

$$ k=\frac{\text{Rate}}{[A]^n} $$

That is why the unit of $k$ changes with order. So statement (3) is correct.

For a first order reaction:

$$ \text{Rate}=k[A] $$

So,

$$ k=\frac{\text{Rate}}{[A]} $$

$$ k=\frac{\mathrm{M s}^{-1}}{\mathrm{M}}=\mathrm{s}^{-1} $$

So the unit of $k$ for a first order reaction is $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, not $\mathrm{M s}^{-1}$.

Hence statement (4) is incorrect.

So, the number of correct statements is:

$$ \boxed{3} $$

en.content: In the presence of acid, the initial concentration, of cane-sugar was reduced from 0.2 M to 0.1 M in 5 hr and to 0.05 M in 10 hr. What will be the order of reaction
en.explanation:
The concentration of cane sugar changes like this:

$$0.2\,M \rightarrow 0.1\,M \text{ in } 5 \text{ hr}$$

This means the concentration becomes half in $5$ hours.

Again,

$$0.1\,M \rightarrow 0.05\,M \text{ in next } 5 \text{ hr}$$

Again the concentration becomes half in $5$ hours.

So the half-life is constant:

$$t_{1/2}=5 \text{ hr}$$

For a first-order reaction, the half-life is independent of the initial concentration. It is given by

$$t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}$$

Since the half-life remains the same even when the concentration changes, the reaction is of first order.

So, the order of the reaction is

$$\boxed{1}$$

en.content: A flask contains a mixture of compounds A and B. Both compounds decompose by first-order kinetics. The half-lives for $A$ and $B$ are 300 s and 180 s, respectively. If the concentrations of $A$ and $B$ are equal initially, the time required for the concentration of $A$ to be four times that of $B$ (in $s$ ) is $\ldots \ldots($ Use $\ln 2=0.693)$
en.explanation:
For a first-order reaction, the rate constant is related to half-life by

$$ k=\frac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} $$

For compound $A$,

$$ k_A=\frac{0.693}{300} $$

For compound $B$,

$$ k_B=\frac{0.693}{180} $$

Since $B$ has a smaller half-life, it decomposes faster than $A$. So after some time, concentration of $A$ becomes greater than that of $B$.

For first-order decomposition,

$$ [A]=[A]_0e^{-k_A t} $$

and

$$ [B]=[B]_0e^{-k_B t} $$

Given initially concentrations are equal:

$$ [A]_0=[B]_0 $$

We need the time when

$$ [A]=4[B] $$

So,

$$ \frac{[A]}{[B]}=4 $$

Substituting the first-order expressions:

$$ \frac{[A]_0e^{-k_A t}}{[B]_0e^{-k_B t}}=4 $$

Since $[A]_0=[B]_0$,

$$ e^{(k_B-k_A)t}=4 $$

Taking natural logarithm on both sides:

$$ (k_B-k_A)t=\ln 4 $$

Now,

$$ k_B-k_A=\frac{0.693}{180}-\frac{0.693}{300} $$

$$ k_B-k_A=0.693\left(\frac{1}{180}-\frac{1}{300}\right) $$

$$ k_B-k_A=0.693\left(\frac{300-180}{180 \times 300}\right) $$

$$ k_B-k_A=0.693\left(\frac{120}{54000}\right) $$

$$ k_B-k_A=\frac{0.693}{450} $$

Also,

$$ \ln 4=\ln 2^2=2\ln 2=2(0.693) $$

So,

$$ t=\frac{2(0.693)}{0.693/450} $$

$$ t=900 \ \text{s} $$

The required time is

$$ \boxed{900 \ \text{s}} $$

en.content: For a first order reaction, the ratio of the time for $80 \%$ completion of a reaction to the time for $50 \%$ completion is $\_\_\_\_$.
en.explanation:
For any first order reaction, the time taken to reach a certain amount of completion is given by

$$t=\frac{2.303}{k}\log\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}$$

Here $[A]_0$ is the starting amount and $[A]$ is the amount left after some reaction has happened. Let us take the starting amount as 100.

When the reaction is $80\%$ complete, $80$ parts have reacted and $20$ parts are left. So the time for this is

$$t_{80\%}=\frac{2.303}{k}\log\frac{100}{100-80}=\frac{2.303}{k}\log\frac{100}{20}$$

When the reaction is $50\%$ complete, $50$ parts have reacted and $50$ parts are left. So the time for this is

$$t_{50\%}=\frac{2.303}{k}\log\frac{100}{100-50}=\frac{2.303}{k}\log\frac{100}{50}$$

Now we take the ratio of these two times. Notice that $\frac{2.303}{k}$ appears in both, so it cancels out and we are left only with the log terms.

$$\frac{t_{80\%}}{t_{50\%}}=\frac{\log 100-\log 20}{\log 100-\log 50}$$

Putting in the values of the logs, the top comes out as $0.6989$ and the bottom as $0.3010$.

$$\frac{t_{80\%}}{t_{50\%}}=\frac{0.6989}{0.3010}=2$$

So the time needed for $80\%$ completion is exactly twice the time needed for $50\%$ completion. The ratio is $2$.

en.content: The rate coefficient ( $k$ ) for a particular reactions is $1.3 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, and $1.3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at $150^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The energy of activation $\left(E_A\right)$ (in kJ for this reaction is $\_\_\_\_$ (nearest integer)
en.explanation:
Using Arrhenius equation for two temperatures,

$$ \log \frac{k_2}{k_1}=\frac{E_A}{2.303R}\left(\frac{T_2-T_1}{T_1T_2}\right) $$

Given,

$$ k_1=1.3\times 10^{-4}\ \text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1} $$

at

$$ T_1=100^\circ\text{C}=373\ \text{K} $$

and

$$ k_2=1.3\times 10^{-3}\ \text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1} $$

at

$$ T_2=150^\circ\text{C}=423\ \text{K} $$

Now,

$$ \frac{k_2}{k_1}=\frac{1.3\times 10^{-3}}{1.3\times 10^{-4}}=10 $$

So,

$$ \log \frac{k_2}{k_1}=\log 10=1 $$

Substituting the values,

$$ 1=\frac{E_A}{2.303\times 8.314}\left(\frac{423-373}{373\times 423}\right) $$

$$ 1=\frac{E_A}{19.147}\left(\frac{50}{157779}\right) $$

So,

$$ E_A=19.147\times \frac{157779}{50} $$

$$ E_A\approx 60435\ \text{J mol}^{-1} $$

Converting into kJ mol$^{-1}$,

$$ E_A\approx 60.4\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} $$

Nearest integer:

$$ \boxed{60} $$
